How Going Public Works and What It Means for Investors What Is an IPO? How Going Public Works and What It Means for Investors By ModernWallet Research Desk · Reviewed by Jonathan Teplitsky, MBA · Updated November 25, 2026 · How we review An IPO, or initial public offering, happens when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time and lists on a stock exchange. Going public raises cash and creates a tradable stock, but it also brings added costs, disclosure requirements, and outside pressure that a private company never faces. This guide explains how a company actually goes public, the real benefits and downsides, and the details most overviews skip: lockup expirations, why retail investors rarely get first-day access, and how to avoid chasing IPO hype. Tools for this journey Investing → Portfolio → Private companies vs public companies A private company is owned by a small group — founders, employees, and private investors — and has no obligation to disclose its finances to the public. A public company sells shares on a stock exchange that anyone can buy, and in exchange it must regularly file detailed financial reports with the SEC , including quarterly and annual reports. Going from private to public changes more than who owns the stock. It exposes the company's financials, strategy, and executive pay to competitors, analysts, and short sellers, all watching every quarterly report. Some founders treat that scrutiny as the price of access to public capital; others see it as a reason to stay private as long as they can. How a company goes public: the IPO process A company goes public by hiring investment banks, called underwriters, to manage the offering, then filing a detailed registration statement with the SEC — searchable on the SEC's EDGAR system — that discloses its financials, risks, and business model. The SEC reviews the filing and can require changes before the offering proceeds. Once the filing clears review, the company and its underwriters go on a roadshow, pitching the stock to large institutional investors to gauge demand. That demand helps set the IPO price the night before trading begins. On the first trading day, the stock starts trading on the exchange, and its price can move sharply away from the IPO price within hours. The real benefits of going public Going public gives a company a large, one-time cash infusion it can use to pay down debt, fund growth, or acquire other companies. A public listing also creates a liquid stock that lets employees and early investors finally sell shares they've held for years, and it gives the company a public currency — its own stock — to use for future acquisitions. A public listing can also raise a company's profile with customers and partners, since a stock ticker carries a kind of credibility a private company doesn't have. For many founders and early employees, an IPO is the main way years of equity compensation finally turns into cash. Why an IPO can actually be a bad idea for the company Going public isn't automatically the right move, and plenty of successful companies choose to stay private for exactly that reason. The ongoing costs are real: compliance, quarterly reporting, investor relations staff, and far more exposure to shareholder lawsuits than a private company ever faces. Public markets also pressure management toward short-term results, since missing a single quarterly earnings estimate can hit the stock hard, even when the long-term strategy is sound. A company that needs years to execute a plan may find that pressure genuinely destructive, which is why some late-stage private companies raise plenty of cash from private investors and delay going public for as long as they can. How IPOs actually work for retail investors Retail investors — individuals buying through an ordinary brokerage account — almost never get shares at the IPO price on day one. The SEC's investor bulletin on IPOs notes that underwriters distribute most IPO shares to their institutional and high-net-worth clients first, so most retail investors can only buy once the stock starts trading on the open market, often at a price already well above the IPO price. A second risk shows up months later: the lockup period. Company insiders and early investors typically sign a lockup agreement , most commonly 180 days, that bars them from selling shares right after the IPO. When that lockup expires, a wave of insider selling can hit the stock all at once — the expiration date is disclosed in the prospectus, so retail investors can see it coming and plan around it instead of being surprised. The first-day 'pop' also isn't guaranteed to hold. A stock that jumps 40% on day one can just as easily give that gain back, or fall below its IPO price entirely, in the weeks and months that follow, once the initial demand from underpricing and hype fades. Once a company lists, you buy it like any other stock; SpaceX, which began trading on Nasdaq as SPCX on June 12, 2026, is a recent example, and our guide on how to buy SpaceX stock now that it's public walks through the order. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 and began trading on Nasdaq as ANT on November 19, 2026; our guide on how to buy Anthropic stock covers the post-IPO price and lock-up details. Tips for investing in IPOs without chasing the hype Read the prospectus before you buy, not the headlines about the deal. The SEC recommends studying the actual offering document, since it discloses the company's finances, risks, and how shares are being allocated, in far more detail than any news story will. Watch for recency and hype bias: a stock dominating your social feed the week of its IPO is exactly the stock priced for maximum optimism, which leaves the least room for good news to push it higher. Waiting for the lockup expiration to pass, and for a full quarter or two of public reporting, gives you real financial data to evaluate instead of a roadshow pitch. Size any single IPO position small relative to your overall portfolio. A single new stock, with no trading history and a wave of insider selling still ahead of it, carries far more risk than an established company — our portfolio calculator can help you see how one volatile position affects your overall risk before you buy. Frequently asked questions What does IPO mean? IPO stands for initial public offering, the first time a private company sells shares to the public and begins trading on a stock exchange. Before the IPO, the company's shares are held by founders, employees, and private investors. Can regular investors buy shares at the IPO price? Rarely. Underwriters distribute most IPO shares to institutional and high-net-worth clients before trading opens, so most retail investors buy on the open market once trading begins, often at a price already above the IPO price. What is an IPO lockup period? A lockup period is a set window, most commonly 180 days, during which company insiders and early investors agree not to sell their shares after the IPO. When the lockup expires, a surge of insider selling can push the stock price down. Why do IPO stocks sometimes drop after their first day? A first-day 'pop' often reflects initial hype and intentional underpricing by underwriters, not the company's long-term value. As that early demand fades and the lockup expiration approaches, the stock can give back its early gains or fall below its IPO price. Why would a company avoid going public? Going public adds ongoing costs — compliance, quarterly reporting, investor relations, and shareholder lawsuit exposure — plus pressure to hit short-term earnings targets. Some companies with long-term strategies choose to stay private and raise cash from private investors instead. Is it risky to invest in a company's IPO? Yes, IPOs carry more risk than established public stocks because there's little public trading history, and a wave of insider selling is often still ahead at the lockup expiration. Reading the prospectus, sizing the position small, and waiting past the initial hype all help manage that risk. What is the difference between an IPO and a stock? An IPO is an event where a private company sells shares to the public for the first time, while a stock is the actual share of ownership you hold. Once that offering concludes, those same shares trade on the open market as ordinary public stock. The practical difference for buyers comes down to access and pricing. Underwriters set the IPO price the night before trading begins and distribute most of those initial shares to institutional and high-net-worth clients first. Most retail investors must wait until trading opens on the exchange, where they often pay a price already above that initial offering figure. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) describes the Marketplace as the place to find private health insurance options, buy a plan, and get help with premiums and out-of-pocket costs for those who are eligible. Monthly premiums for a Marketplace plan go directly to the insurance company. Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) provide free or low-cost coverage to eligible low-income adults, families and children, pregnant women, the elderly, and people with disabilities, according to HealthCare.gov. Medicaid programs must follow federal guidelines, but eligible income levels, coverage and costs differ from state to state. Some Medicaid programs pay for care directly, and others use private insurance companies to provide Medicaid coverage. Benefits also follow different rules. Full-benefit Medicaid benefits differ by state, though HealthCare.gov says all states provide comprehensive coverage. Every Marketplace plan covers 10 benefit categories, including prescription drugs, emergency services, hospitalization, laboratory services, and mental health and substance use disorder services, along with pre-existing conditions and free preventive services from in-network providers. Marketplace plans and full-benefit Medicaid count as qualifying health coverage. HealthCare.gov lists Marketplace plans, Medicaid and CHIP among the coverage types that meet the law's minimum requirements for comprehensive health coverage. The IRS lists this as a premium tax credit condition: the person enrolled in Marketplace coverage must not be eligible for coverage through a government program such as Medicaid or CHIP. HealthCare.gov puts it plainly: "If you qualify for Medicaid, you aren't eligible for savings on a Marketplace plan." Declining Medicaid does not restore the savings. A person eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP who keeps a Marketplace plan generally pays full price for the premium and for covered services. A child may also lose CHIP eligibility if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is one exception. Some limited types of Medicaid pay only for family planning, treatment of an emergency medical condition, or tuberculosis services. When a Medicaid program does not count as minimum essential coverage, the person may be eligible for premium tax credits and other Marketplace savings if they qualify based on income and other criteria. HealthCare.gov's Medicaid minimum essential coverage lookup shows, by state, whether a given Medicaid program counts and what action to take. People with limited Medicaid can also fill out a Marketplace application to find out whether they qualify for full-benefit Medicaid or a Marketplace plan with savings. Medicaid status is one of several federal tests. The IRS lists these premium tax credit requirements: Household income generally from 100 percent to 400 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL) for the family size. A filing status other than married filing separately, apart from a special rule for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. Not being claimable as a dependent by another person. No access to affordable employer coverage that provides minimum value for the person enrolled. Payment of the share of premiums not covered by advance credit payments. A timing rule applies when status changes mid-year. The Marketplace may find someone ineligible for Medicaid at enrollment and approve advance credit payments. In that case, the IRS generally treats the person as ineligible for Medicaid for the rest of the plan year, even if Medicaid later approves coverage. The IRS still tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately. ACA vs Medicaid Income Rules Household income alone does not decide whether a person gets Medicaid or Marketplace savings, because state rules and personal categories change the result. HealthCare.gov says each state's coverage options consider income, household size, family status such as pregnancy or caring for young children, disability, age and other factors. Some states expanded Medicaid to cover adults below a certain income level, and others did not. HealthCare.gov advises applying for Medicaid even when income looks too high. That advice applies especially to people who have children, are pregnant or have a disability. The federal poverty level is a yearly income measure used for both programs. HealthCare.gov's federal poverty level table lists 2026 amounts of $15,960 for one person and $33,000 for a family of four, with higher amounts in Alaska and Hawaii. Under HealthCare.gov's general bands, income below 138 percent of FPL may qualify for Medicaid in an expansion state. Income below 100 percent probably will not qualify for Marketplace savings but may qualify for Medicaid. Marketplace savings use expected household modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). Medicaid income rules vary by state and eligibility category. HealthCare.gov's income guide defines MAGI as adjusted gross income plus untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits and tax-exempt interest, without Supplemental Security Income. Marketplace savings are based on expected household income for the coverage year rather than last year's income. Self-employed applicants count the income they expect to make from the business after expenses. For income that is hard to predict, HealthCare.gov says to report current income, review the yearly estimate it shows, and update the application as changes happen. For tax years after 2025, the IRS applies no repayment cap. The full amount of advance credit payments above the allowed credit is added to the tax bill. Members of one household can end up in different programs. HealthCare.gov notes that children may qualify for CHIP even when a parent does not qualify for Medicaid. In many cases, a parent who qualifies for Marketplace savings will have children who qualify for Medicaid or CHIP. Applying Through the Marketplace or Your State A household can apply for Medicaid through a Marketplace application or directly through its state Medicaid agency, and either route can lead to the other program. On a Marketplace application, if anyone in the household looks eligible for Medicaid or CHIP, the Marketplace securely sends that information to the state agency, which then contacts the household about enrollment. The same Marketplace application shows whether anyone qualifies for cost savings on a Marketplace plan. The direct route starts with the state. HealthCare.gov's Medicaid and CHIP coverage page lists contact information for each state's Medicaid agency. A state denial feeds back into the Marketplace. In most cases, the state securely sends the person's contact information to the Marketplace, which mails a letter about Marketplace coverage. A denied applicant can apply and enroll in Marketplace coverage without waiting for that letter. Enrollment timing differs between the two: Medicaid and CHIP: apply any time of year, and coverage can start immediately. Marketplace Open Enrollment: November 1 to January 15. Enroll by December 15 for coverage that starts January 1, or by January 15 for coverage that starts February 1. Marketplace outside Open Enrollment: a qualifying life change opens a Special Enrollment Period. Medicaid may also help pay for medical care from the last 3 months, even before enrollment. Payment depends on the family's income and medical expenses at the time care was received. Marketplace applications can be filed online, by phone, with help from someone in the community, through an agent or broker, through certified enrollment partner websites, or on paper. HealthCare.gov offers a checklist of what to gather before applying on its Marketplace quick guide . Rules to Check for 2027 Coverage Two rule changes shape 2027 coverage decisions: a Medicaid work requirement in some states and immigration-status rules for full Medicaid and Marketplace savings. Both notices appear on HealthCare.gov's Medicaid and CHIP coverage page and its Marketplace quick guide . Starting January 1, 2027, adults in states that provide Medicaid based on income alone may need to meet a new monthly work requirement to qualify for Medicaid or keep it. A state that elected CMS's optional hold harmless period may pause denials and disenrollments for missing it through June 30, 2027, as our guide to Medicaid work requirement rules for 2027 explains. HealthCare.gov says a person who lost or was denied Medicaid for not meeting the state's work requirement may get Marketplace coverage. That person will not qualify for savings to lower Marketplace plan costs. After an ordinary Medicaid denial, by contrast, HealthCare.gov says a person may qualify for the premium tax credit or other cost savings. The reason for a Medicaid denial therefore matters for the Marketplace budget. A household comparing plans after a work-requirement denial should expect full-price premiums when estimating monthly costs. For noncitizen applicants, HealthCare.gov lists these immigration statuses for full Medicaid or CHIP coverage following a law change: Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR, Green Card holder) Cuban or Haitian entrant Compact of Free Association (COFA) migrant Depending on the state, lawfully residing pregnant women and children may also be eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP. For noncitizens applying for Marketplace plans, only certain immigration statuses qualify for savings starting January 1, 2027. People with other statuses may still be eligible for Marketplace coverage without savings. For 2027 Marketplace coverage starting January 1, the enrollment deadline is December 15. Medicaid applications remain open year-round. The Next Step Before Choosing a Plan The next step is an official eligibility result for each person in the household, from a Marketplace application on HealthCare.gov or from the state Medicaid agency. That result answers the ACA vs Medicaid question person by person. Full-benefit Medicaid eligibility generally removes Marketplace savings. Limited-benefit Medicaid, an ordinary Medicaid denial and a work-requirement denial can lead to different savings outcomes. Neither option is the better choice for every household, because eligibility rules decide which coverage comes with financial help. If the result points to a Marketplace plan, compare each plan's monthly premium and provider network in the Marketplace before enrolling. A Marketplace plan starts only after the first premium is paid, if there is one. If you already have coverage, confirm replacement coverage before ending the existing plan. If Medicaid is approved while a Marketplace plan is active, HealthCare.gov says to end the Marketplace plan when Medicaid starts, unless you tell the state agency you want to keep both. Once the premium is known, plan the monthly premium alongside other bills. If income changes month to month, budget insurance with irregular income . Update your Marketplace income estimate whenever expected income changes, then check how that affects your ACA vs Medicaid coverage. Frequently Asked Questions What is Obamacare insurance? Obamacare is another name for the Affordable Care Act (ACA), a law. Marketplace plans are private health insurance bought through the Health Insurance Marketplace. Every Marketplace plan covers 10 benefit categories, including prescription drugs, emergency services and hospitalization, and covers pre-existing conditions. Depending on expected household income, a buyer may qualify for a premium tax credit that lowers the monthly premium, plus extra savings on deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. Medicaid is a separate public program run jointly by the federal government and the states. What is a coverage gap in health insurance? In a state that has not expanded Medicaid, a coverage gap means some adults cannot get Medicaid or ordinary Marketplace savings. HealthCare.gov describes adults below 100% of the federal poverty level who do not qualify under their state's Medicaid rules. Their incomes are too high for Medicaid in their state and too low for ordinary Marketplace savings. A 2027 Medicaid work-requirement denial can also prevent Marketplace savings, but it follows a separate rule. Still apply, because state categories and other factors can change the outcome. What disqualifies you for Medicaid? No single factor disqualifies everyone, because each state sets its own Medicaid income levels and categories within federal guidelines. Income above a category's limit can prevent Medicaid eligibility. For noncitizen applicants, immigration status also affects full-coverage eligibility. A state that has not expanded Medicaid may offer fewer coverage options. Starting January 1, 2027, adults in states that cover people based on income alone may lose or be denied Medicaid for not meeting a monthly work requirement. HealthCare.gov still recommends applying when income looks too high, especially for people with children, a pregnancy or a disability. Is ACA or Medicaid better? Neither is better for every household, because eligibility rules decide which option comes with financial help. A person eligible for full-benefit Medicaid gets free or low-cost coverage there, and would generally pay full price for a Marketplace plan. A person denied Medicaid for ordinary reasons may qualify for a premium tax credit on a Marketplace plan, while a 2027 work-requirement denial allows Marketplace coverage without savings. Full-benefit Medicaid coverage differs by state. Every state provides comprehensive full-benefit coverage, and every Marketplace plan covers the same 10 benefit categories. Compare actual premiums and provider networks after the eligibility result arrives. Can you have Medicaid and Marketplace insurance at the same time? Yes, a person can keep both, but full-benefit Medicaid generally means paying full price for the Marketplace plan premium and covered services. HealthCare.gov says to tell the state agency if you want to keep both, and notes that a child may no longer qualify for CHIP if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is different: a person may still qualify for Marketplace savings based on income and other factors. The IRS tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately. mainEntity.name: What is Obamacare insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Obamacare is another name for the Affordable Care Act (ACA), a law. Marketplace plans are private health insurance bought through the Health Insurance Marketplace. Every Marketplace plan covers 10 benefit categories, including prescription drugs, emergency services and hospitalization, and covers pre-existing conditions. Depending on expected household income, a buyer may qualify for a premium tax credit that lowers the monthly premium, plus extra savings on deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. Medicaid is a separate public program run jointly by the federal government and the states.

mainEntity.name: What is a coverage gap in health insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: In a state that has not expanded Medicaid, a coverage gap means some adults cannot get Medicaid or ordinary Marketplace savings. HealthCare.gov describes adults below 100% of the federal poverty level who do not qualify under their state's Medicaid rules. Their incomes are too high for Medicaid in their state and too low for ordinary Marketplace savings. A 2027 Medicaid work-requirement denial can also prevent Marketplace savings, but it follows a separate rule. Still apply, because state categories and other factors can change the outcome.

mainEntity.name: What disqualifies you for Medicaid?

acceptedAnswer.text: No single factor disqualifies everyone, because each state sets its own Medicaid income levels and categories within federal guidelines. Income above a category's limit can prevent Medicaid eligibility. For noncitizen applicants, immigration status also affects full-coverage eligibility. A state that has not expanded Medicaid may offer fewer coverage options. Starting January 1, 2027, adults in states that cover people based on income alone may lose or be denied Medicaid for not meeting a monthly work requirement. HealthCare.gov still recommends applying when income looks too high, especially for people with children, a pregnancy or a disability.

mainEntity.name: Is ACA or Medicaid better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither is better for every household, because eligibility rules decide which option comes with financial help. A person eligible for full-benefit Medicaid gets free or low-cost coverage there, and would generally pay full price for a Marketplace plan. A person denied Medicaid for ordinary reasons may qualify for a premium tax credit on a Marketplace plan, while a 2027 work-requirement denial allows Marketplace coverage without savings. Full-benefit Medicaid coverage differs by state. Every state provides comprehensive full-benefit coverage, and every Marketplace plan covers the same 10 benefit categories. Compare actual premiums and provider networks after the eligibility result arrives.

mainEntity.name: Can you have Medicaid and Marketplace insurance at the same time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a person can keep both, but full-benefit Medicaid generally means paying full price for the Marketplace plan premium and covered services. HealthCare.gov says to tell the state agency if you want to keep both, and notes that a child may no longer qualify for CHIP if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is different: a person may still qualify for Marketplace savings based on income and other factors. The IRS tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately.

Enter your expected 2027 household income in the calculator below. Run it again with a plausible lower estimate and a plausible higher estimate. The Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF) 2027 enrollment analysis says accurate income estimates matter especially near the thresholds for premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions. Locate the 400% federal poverty level (FPL) line. The ordinary premium tax credit range is 100% to 400% of FPL. Above 400% of FPL, there is no federal premium tax credit under the rules KFF describes for 2027. If your income is within the eligible range, your credit may be smaller than it would have been under the enhanced credits that expired at the end of 2025. KFF reports that finalized 2027 benchmark silver premiums rose 13% on average. Compare bronze with silver beyond the monthly premium. Bronze plans have lower premiums and higher deductibles. KFF reports that the average Marketplace deductible rose 37%, from $2,759 in 2025 to $3,786 in 2026, largely as more people selected bronze instead of silver plans with reduced deductibles. Those figures describe 2026 compared with 2025; they are not a forecast of your 2027 deductible. If your income is 100% to 250% of FPL, check the silver plan's cost-sharing reductions (CSRs) before choosing bronze. CSRs can lower deductibles, copayments and coinsurance, but require enrollment in a silver plan. Treat catastrophic coverage as a limited possibility. KFF says that, during open enrollment, catastrophic plans are available only to a narrow group. Eligibility includes people under 30, people whose Marketplace or employer coverage would cost more than 8.5% of their income, and people who qualify for a hardship exemption. Do not count on a catastrophic plan until you know whether you meet one of those conditions. Enroll by your exchange's deadline. HealthCare.gov says to enroll by December 15 for January 1 coverage. Its open enrollment ends January 15; enrollment or plan changes after that generally require a Special Enrollment Period. State-run exchanges can set different dates, so use the deadline shown by the exchange handling your application. A cheaper plan can lower your payment, but it cannot restore a credit you do not qualify for. The credit is based on the benchmark silver premium minus an income-based contribution and cannot exceed the premium of the plan you choose. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) describes the credit this way. Revenue Procedure 2026-26 sets the 2027 percentages used for the contribution. The calculator runs five steps: Divide expected 2027 household MAGI by the 2026 federal poverty level (FPL) for your household size. Find that percentage of FPL in the 2027 table below, and interpolate in a straight line inside its band. Multiply MAGI by the applicable percentage, then divide by 12 for the monthly contribution. Subtract the monthly contribution from the monthly benchmark premium. A negative result counts as zero. Cap the result at the monthly premium of the plan you choose. Written as one line, the credit is the smaller of two numbers: your plan premium, or the benchmark minus your contribution (never below zero). At 231.05% of FPL, income sits 31.05 points into the 50-point band from 200% to 250%. The rate climbs the same share of the way from 6.78% to 8.66%, which lands at about 7.95%. The calculator keeps the dollar result hidden until you confirm the nonfinancial conditions listed under When the ACA Subsidy Calculator Does Not Apply. Below 100% or above 400% of FPL, it shows an explanation in place of a credit. It estimates the federal credit only, with no state subsidy and no estimate of discounts on your share of costs for covered services. Income for the 2027 ACA Subsidy Calculator Enter your household's expected MAGI for 2027, the full year you want coverage. HealthCare.gov states that Marketplace savings are based on expected household income for the coverage year. Last year's income is only a starting point: the HealthCare.gov glossary says to begin with your most recent adjusted gross income (AGI) and adjust it for expected changes. MAGI does not appear as a line on your tax return. Build it in two steps: Start with AGI, which is line 11 of IRS Form 1040 . Add untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits, and tax-exempt interest. Leave out Supplemental Security Income (SSI). For many people, MAGI equals AGI or comes close. Take-home pay alone is the wrong input for this calculator. If your pay stub lists federal taxable wages, use that number. If it does not, HealthCare.gov says to start from gross income and subtract what your employer takes out for child care, health coverage, and retirement plans. Self-employment income goes in after business expenses. Some money stays out of the estimate entirely: child support gifts loan proceeds, such as student loans or home equity loans SSI veterans' disability payments workers' compensation Household size and household income follow tax rules. Your family for the credit is you, your spouse if you file jointly, and everyone you claim as a dependent, including dependents who do not need coverage. Household income adds the MAGI of each family member who is required to file a federal return, so a teenager's summer-job pay counts only if that teen must file. The coverage family is a smaller group. The IRS defines it as the family members enrolled through the Marketplace who cannot get Medicaid , Medicare, or affordable employer coverage. Enter the full tax household size and income, and use a benchmark premium that applies to the coverage family. ACA Subsidy Income Limits for 2027 For 2027 coverage, the ordinary federal premium tax credit range is household income from 100% to 400% of the 2026 federal poverty level for your household size. The IRS bases each year's credit on the poverty guidelines most recently published when open enrollment begins, so the 2025 credit used 2024 figures and the 2027 credit uses 2026 figures. The rule that allowed credits above 400% applied to tax years 2021 through 2025 only. The 2027 table runs to "not more than 400%," so a two-person household at exactly $86,560 stays inside the range. In our calculation, that household's contribution is 10.22% of income, or $737.20 a month, and an illustrative $1,000 benchmark with a $1,000 plan premium leaves a $262.80 monthly credit. Add $1 of income and the same household reaches 400.0046% of FPL, which removes the credit in the ordinary federal model. If your income sits near the line, run the calculator at both your low and high estimates before you count on the credit. The table shows an income window. It does not establish eligibility by itself. HealthCare.gov says income below 100% of FPL probably will not qualify for Marketplace savings but may qualify for Medicaid, and income below 138% may qualify for Medicaid in states that expanded it. The calculator covers households of 1 to 8 people in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia (DC). Poverty guidelines are higher in Alaska and Hawaii, and the 2026 table adds $5,680 for each person past eight. Households in either group should rely on the Marketplace application for their figure. The Benchmark and Your Chosen Plan The benchmark is the monthly premium for the second-lowest-cost Silver plan that applies to your coverage family, and it sets the size of the credit. Your chosen plan's premium, which the IRS calls the enrollment premium, acts only as a ceiling. The calculator asks for both numbers because they do different jobs in the formula. The IRS settles two edge cases for the benchmark. If only one Silver plan is available where you live, that plan counts as the second-lowest-cost Silver plan. If the two cheapest Silver plans cost the same, that shared premium is the benchmark. Tobacco use changes only one of the two inputs. The benchmark leaves out tobacco surcharges, so enter the non-tobacco price. The enrollment premium is the amount you are charged, so a tobacco user enters the higher plan price. The IRS gives an example of both rules. A $900 non-smoker benchmark is used even though smokers are quoted $1,200 for that plan. A tobacco user charged $650 for the chosen plan uses $650 as the enrollment premium, even though the non-tobacco price is $500. The ceiling comes into play when you pick a cheaper plan. If the benchmark minus your contribution is more than your plan's premium, the credit stops at that premium. The calculator has no ZIP code database and no built-in prices. Its $600 benchmark and $550 plan defaults are hypothetical numbers for the arithmetic. When you apply, the Marketplace estimates your credit from your family size, projected income, and other coverage, and the plan prices it shows are the figures to enter here. A Worked Federal Premium-Credit Calculation In our calculation, a two-person household with $50,000 of expected 2027 MAGI, a $600 benchmark, and a $550 chosen plan gets a $268.85 monthly federal credit and pays $281.15 a month. Both premiums are illustrative and come from no ZIP code quote. The arithmetic assumes every other eligibility condition is met. Step Figure 2026 FPL for 2 people $21,640 Income as % of FPL 231.05% Applicable percentage about 7.95% Yearly contribution $3,973.81 Monthly contribution $331.15 Benchmark minus contribution $600 minus $331.15 = $268.85 Cap check against the $550 plan $268.85 is under the cap Monthly credit $268.85 Net monthly premium $550 minus $268.85 = $281.15 A second case shows the premium cap. Use two people with $30,000 of MAGI, a $900 benchmark, and a $100 monthly plan premium. Assume every other eligibility condition is met, including that no one is eligible for Medicaid. Income is 138.63% of FPL, the applicable percentage is about 3.58%, and the monthly contribution is $89.61. The benchmark minus that contribution is far more than the $100 plan premium. The credit cannot exceed the $100 plan premium, so the credit is $100 and the net premium is $0. Read together, the two cases show how each input works. Income sets the contribution. When the ACA Subsidy Calculator Does Not Apply The calculator's figure does not apply to anyone eligible for government coverage that counts as qualifying health coverage, anyone with affordable employer coverage, or a household that fails the IRS filing rules. The calculator asks you to confirm these conditions before it shows a credit. Government coverage: a person eligible for Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) , Medicare, or another government program that counts as qualifying health coverage cannot get the credit for that person's Marketplace coverage. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count is an exception. Employer offers: an offer for 2027 plan years is generally affordable if the employee's self-only premium share is no more than 10.22% of household income. The test uses the lowest-cost plan that covers at least 60% of expected costs, and family members' offers apply the same percentage to the family premium. Employer enrollment: enrolling in an employer plan, including retiree coverage, blocks the credit even if that plan is unaffordable. Coverage from a former employer, including retiree coverage, can be declined, and the credit may still be available. Filing rules: married couples who file separately generally cannot claim the credit, with an exception for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. A person who can be claimed as a dependent by someone else cannot claim it. A new Medicaid rule starts January 1, 2027, which our guide covers as Medicaid work requirements starting 2027 . HealthCare.gov says states that cover adults based on income alone may require a monthly work requirement for Medicaid. A person who lost or was denied Medicaid for not meeting that requirement may get Marketplace coverage but will not qualify for savings. Leave eligibility unconfirmed in the calculator to show an explanation instead of a credit. Limited Medicaid works differently. Some programs pay only for family planning, emergency treatment, or tuberculosis services. If your state's program does not count as qualifying health coverage , you may still get the premium tax credit when you meet the income and other rules. The calculator does not evaluate immigration status or state programs. Three facts can reverse an estimate: an affordable employer offer, eligibility for Medicaid or another government program that counts as qualifying coverage, and changes in law or plan prices. The official next step is a Marketplace application . HealthCare.gov says the application sends your information to your state if anyone in the household may qualify for Medicaid or CHIP. It also tells you whether you qualify for savings on a Marketplace plan. Updating Income Before Tax Reconciliation Advance payments of the premium tax credit are an estimate, and your final 2027 credit is figured on your tax return from actual household income and family size. If the advance payments were larger than the final credit, the IRS sets no repayment cap for tax years after 2025. The full difference reduces your refund or raises your balance due, and if the final credit is larger, the difference goes to you. Reporting changes to the Marketplace as soon as they happen lets it adjust your advance payments. The IRS lists these events among those that can change the credit: a lump-sum Social Security or Social Security Disability Insurance payment a taxable lump-sum distribution from an individual retirement account or other retirement arrangement capital gains from selling stocks, bonds, or cryptocurrency canceled debt, such as forgiven credit card debt marriage, divorce, a birth or adoption, or a move gaining or losing eligibility for employer or government coverage Filing a return is required. Anyone with advance payments must file a federal return with Form 8962 , and skipping that return ends advance payments in future years. Plan the premium around a range of incomes. Run the calculator at a low and a high 2027 income estimate, compare the two net premiums, and set aside the difference if your income can swing. Our guide on how to budget with irregular income covers health insurance costs without an employer plan, and you can put the premium in a household budget . The estimate requires a correct benchmark premium and annual MAGI. Take-home pay alone cannot establish annual MAGI. An affordable employer offer, qualifying government coverage, or changed law or plan prices can reverse it. Compare income scenarios in the ACA subsidy calculator, then update your Marketplace application whenever your income changes. Frequently Asked Questions What is ACA subsidy based on? The ACA premium tax credit is based on expected household modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) compared with the federal poverty level for your household size, plus the benchmark Silver premium for your coverage family. The income sets your contribution, the benchmark minus that contribution sets the credit, and the premium of the plan you enroll in caps it. How to qualify for ACA subsidy? You must meet every IRS eligibility condition. Income alone cannot establish eligibility. Household income must fall in the allowed range. Married filing separately generally prevents the credit, with a limited abuse or abandonment exception. No one else can claim you as a dependent. The covered person must enroll in a non-catastrophic Marketplace plan and lack affordable employer coverage. Eligibility for qualifying government coverage, such as most Medicaid or Medicare, prevents the credit. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count as qualifying coverage is an exception. The covered person must pay the share of premiums the credit does not cover. What is the maximum ACA subsidy? The ACA subsidy can be as large as the full premium of the plan you enroll in, because the IRS caps the credit at enrollment premiums. Below that cap, the size depends on how far the benchmark premium exceeds your income-based contribution. In our lower-income example, two people with $30,000 of MAGI, a $900 benchmark, and a $100 plan get a $100 credit and pay $0, assuming every other eligibility condition is met. What are the ACA subsidy income limits? For 2027 coverage, the ordinary range is 100% to 400% of the 2026 federal poverty level in the 48 contiguous states and DC. That is $15,960 to $63,840 for one person, $21,640 to $86,560 for two, and $33,000 to $132,000 for four. Alaska and Hawaii use higher poverty guidelines, and income inside the range does not establish eligibility on its own. Is ACA subsidy based on adjusted gross income? The ACA subsidy is based on modified adjusted gross income, which starts with adjusted gross income from line 11 of Form 1040. You add untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits, and tax-exempt interest, and you leave out Supplemental Security Income. For many people the two figures are the same or very close. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. That is $15,960 to $63,840 for one person, $21,640 to $86,560 for two, and $33,000 to $132,000 for four. Alaska and Hawaii use higher poverty guidelines, and income inside the range does not establish eligibility on its own.

mainEntity.name: Is ACA subsidy based on adjusted gross income?

acceptedAnswer.text: The ACA subsidy is based on modified adjusted gross income, which starts with adjusted gross income from line 11 of Form 1040. You add untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits, and tax-exempt interest, and you leave out Supplemental Security Income. For many people the two figures are the same or very close.

Every mortgage also pairs that loan type with a loan term, such as 15 or 30 years, and a rate type, fixed or adjustable. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) frames every home loan this way. Sometimes only one loan type fits your situation. If several fit, the CFPB suggests trying scenarios and asking lenders for several quotes to see which type offers the best deal overall. Tools for this journey Mortgage calculator → Mortgage affordability → FHA loan calculator → VA loan calculator → The Main Types of Mortgage Loans at a Glance Conventional loans make up the majority of mortgages, and the conforming version is the most common loan type. Government and housing agency programs serve specific borrowers, and which type costs least depends on your credit, your down payment and the programs you are eligible for. Loan type Who it is for What to know Conventional (conforming) The majority of loans. Conforming is the most common loan type. The government sets the maximum loan amount, and Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac set the other rules. Mortgage insurance is typically required with less than 20 percent down. Jumbo (non-conforming) Borrowers who need more than the conforming jumbo limit in their county Rules vary by lender. Borrowers usually need good credit and a high down payment. Federal Housing Administration (FHA) Borrowers with lower credit scores or a small down payment Down payments as low as 3.5 percent. Mortgage insurance is required on every FHA loan, and the maximum loan amount varies by county. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Veterans, service members and surviving spouses A Certificate of Eligibility shows the lender you qualify. Nearly 90 percent of VA-backed loans are made with no down payment. U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Low- to middle-income borrowers in rural areas Check eligibility with USDA before applying. State or local housing agency programs Low- to middle-income borrowers, first-time homebuyers or public service employees Offered by state or local housing agencies. Special Purpose Credit Programs are private-lender loans to low- to middle-income borrowers, generally in targeted communities. Three Choices Every Mortgage Combines Every mortgage combines three separate choices: a loan type, a loan term and an interest rate type. Picking a conventional loan does not settle the term or the rate. You still choose those on their own, and each one changes a different part of the deal. Choice Common options What it changes Loan type Conventional, FHA, VA, USDA, special programs Your down payment, your total cost including interest and mortgage insurance, and how much you can borrow Loan term 15 years or 30 years Your monthly payment, your interest rate and your total cost Rate type Fixed or adjustable Whether your principal and interest payment can change over the life of the loan The loan type also affects the house price range you can consider. A 30-year FHA loan and a 15-year FHA loan share a loan type but carry different monthly payments and different total costs. Conforming, Jumbo and Other Conventional Loans A conventional loan is any mortgage that is not part of a specific government program. Conventional loans typically cost less than FHA loans but can be more difficult to get. They split into two main categories, conforming and non-conforming. Conforming loans are the most common loan type. The government sets their maximum loan amounts, and Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, which back conforming loans, set the other rules. By law, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can only buy single-family mortgages below a ceiling called the conforming loan limit. Look up your county's figure on the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) conforming loan limit page before you set a price range. For the 2027 figures and what each down payment buys, see our guide to the 2027 conforming loan limit . The 2026 limits were set using the formula in the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008, and they are higher in some high-cost areas. In certain counties, a conforming jumbo loan covers amounts above the standard limit, with a maximum that varies by county. Jumbo loans above the conforming jumbo limit in your county are non-conforming. Rules vary by lender, but borrowers usually need good credit and a high down payment. Non-conforming loans are less standardized, so eligibility, pricing and features can vary widely, and the CFPB calls shopping around particularly important for them. A third group, other non-conforming loans, covers loans of any size that fit no other category. Some are aimed at borrowers with poor credit and tend to carry high rates. They may also include minimal income documentation, interest-only payments or a balance that is allowed to increase. Many of the loans that got people in trouble during the financial crisis fell in this group. If you are offered one, consult several lenders and ask whether you could qualify for a conforming or FHA loan instead. If a lender pitches a portfolio loan, our portfolio loan explainer walks through how it works. On a conventional loan, a down payment under 20 percent typically means paying for mortgage insurance. Our FHA vs conventional loan comparison is the next read for buyers with a smaller down payment. Government-Backed Loans from FHA, VA and USDA Government-backed loans serve three groups: borrowers with lower credit scores or small down payments (FHA), veterans and service members (VA), and low- to middle-income rural borrowers (USDA). FHA loans come from private lenders and are regulated and insured by the Federal Housing Administration, a government agency that does not lend the money itself. They allow down payments as low as 3.5 percent and lower credit scores than most conventional loans. Mortgage insurance is required on every FHA loan, and the maximum loan amount varies by county. Whether FHA or conventional costs less depends on your profile. For borrowers with good credit and a 10 to 15 percent down payment, FHA loans tend to cost more than conventional loans. For borrowers with lower credit scores or smaller down payments, FHA can often be the cheapest option. The CFPB says there are no hard-and-fast rules and a lot depends on the current market, so ask lenders to quote both. The FHA loan calculator lets you test different down payments before you request quotes. VA home loans help Veterans, service members and their survivors buy, build, improve or refinance a home. VA offers a VA direct loan and 3 VA-backed loans, and nearly 90 percent of VA-backed loans are made with no down payment. A Certificate of Eligibility (COE), based on your service history and duty status, shows a lender that you qualify. A VA loan may offer better terms than a traditional loan from a private bank, mortgage company or credit union. You still need the required credit and income for the amount you borrow. Run your numbers in the VA loan calculator , then read our VA loan vs conventional loan comparison and FHA loan vs VA loan comparison . USDA loans are for low- to middle-income borrowers in rural areas. For how the two programs differ, see our USDA loan vs FHA loan comparison . Fixed-Rate vs Adjustable-Rate Mortgages A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate and the same monthly principal and interest payment. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) has a rate that can rise or fall after an initial period. Most borrowers choose fixed-rate mortgages. On a fixed-rate loan, your total monthly payment can still change if property taxes, homeowner's insurance or mortgage insurance change. An ARM starts with a lower interest rate. Most ARMs have two periods: an introductory period with a fixed rate, then a second period where the rate adjusts regularly. Part of the rate is tied to an index, and the rate you pay is the index plus a set margin, subject to any caps. After the fixed period ends, the monthly principal and interest payment can go up or down. It could go up a lot, even double. Some ARMs include rate caps that limit how much the rate can adjust. An ARM could cost less in the short term, for example if you plan to move within the initial fixed period. If you stay longer than expected, you could pay a lot more. The CFPB warns against assuming you can sell or refinance before the rate changes, because your property's value could drop or your finances could change. Before taking an ARM, get answers to five questions from the lender: How high or low can the rate and payment go with each adjustment? How often does the rate adjust? How soon could the payment go up? Is there a cap on how high the rate can go? Could you still afford the loan at the maximum rate and payment? To weigh the two rate types on cost and risk, read our fixed vs ARM mortgage comparison . Loan Term and the 15-Year vs 30-Year Tradeoff A shorter loan term means higher monthly payments, a typically lower interest rate and a lower total cost. A longer term reverses each of those: lower monthly payments, a typically higher rate and a higher total cost. The CFPB says the rate on a shorter term is usually lower, by as much as a full percentage point. How much lower depends on the terms and rates involved. Rates vary among lenders, especially for shorter terms, so ask each lender to quote both lengths. Our 15-year vs 30-year mortgage comparison covers the two terms, and the 40-year mortgage guide covers a longer term. Loan Features to Question Before You Sign The CFPB flags four loan features to be careful with: a prepayment penalty, a balloon payment, negative amortization and interest-only payments. If a loan offer includes one, ask the loan officer why. Then ask for a second Loan Estimate for the same loan without that feature, so you can see what the feature costs you. Generally, a lender must document and verify your income, employment, assets, debts and credit history to decide whether you can repay. A loan that does this and meets certain criteria may be called a qualified mortgage . Nonqualified mortgages can be riskier or more expensive. They are sometimes marketed to self-employed borrowers or borrowers without Social Security numbers. If you are offered one, compare Loan Estimates from several lenders. How to Compare Types of Mortgage Loans Compare types of mortgage loans by getting official Loan Estimates from several lenders for each type that fits you, then comparing the total cost. The CFPB says never make a final decision about a loan before you have Loan Estimates in hand. Start by narrowing the list on eligibility. A Certificate of Eligibility shows a VA lender that you qualify, and USDA loans are for low- to middle-income rural borrowers. Conforming loans stop at your county's limit, and anything above it is a jumbo loan. Your down payment and credit shape the rest. FHA can often be cheapest with a lower credit score or a small down payment. Conventional tends to cost less with good credit and a 10 to 15 percent down payment. Set a price range with the mortgage affordability calculator , then test terms and rates in the mortgage calculator . Our best mortgage lenders roundup helps you build a shortlist, and our list of questions to ask a mortgage lender covers what to raise on each call. If this is your first purchase, the first-time home buyer guide walks through the steps around the loan. Frequently asked questions What is the most common mortgage type? Conforming conventional loans are the most common type. Conventional loans make up the majority of mortgages, and conforming loans follow maximum loan amounts set by the government plus other rules set by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. On rate type, most borrowers choose a fixed-rate mortgage. What are the five major types of mortgages? The CFPB sorts mortgages into three categories: conventional, government and special programs. Within them, the main loan types are conforming, jumbo, FHA, VA, USDA and state or local housing agency programs. Each type can then pair with a loan term and a fixed or adjustable rate. What is a jumbo mortgage loan? A jumbo mortgage is a loan above the conforming loan limit, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency publishes each year and which varies by county. Some counties allow conforming jumbo loans above the standard limit. Loans above that county figure are non-conforming jumbo loans. What is a hybrid ARM mortgage? A hybrid ARM is an adjustable-rate mortgage that starts with a fixed rate for an introductory period, then adjusts regularly after that. Once adjustments begin, the rate follows an index plus a set margin, subject to any caps, so the monthly payment can rise or fall. The CFPB warns against assuming you can sell or refinance before the rate changes. What are the risks of a mortgage? Risks the CFPB names include rising ARM payments and risky loan features. An ARM payment can go up a lot after the fixed period, even double. Prepayment penalties, balloon payments, negative amortization and interest-only payments all call for caution, and nonqualified mortgages can be riskier or more expensive. Ask for a Loan Estimate without the feature to compare. What is the best type of home mortgage loan? No single type is best for every buyer. The right fit depends on your down payment, your credit, which programs you are eligible for, and how long you plan to stay in the home. How Much Should You Spend on Rent? By ModernWallet Research Desk · Reviewed by Jonathan Teplitsky, MBA · Updated October 26, 2026 · How we review Keep rent at or below 28% of your gross income, and lower once you factor in other debt. The mistake we see readers make most often is applying the 30% rule without checking it against debt payments or take-home pay. That 28% figure comes from the same debt-adjusted 28/36 math lenders use to size a mortgage, but here it's applied to a rent payment instead of a loan. In an expensive metro, that number is not always realistic. The usual fix is a roommate, a smaller unit, or a longer commute, not a bigger rent budget. Tools for this journey Budget → 50/30/20 budget → Where the 30% Rule Came From The 30% rule started as a federal housing benchmark. It was never built as personal budgeting advice. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development ( HUD ) uses 30% of gross income as the line for what it calls "cost burdened" housing. A household above that line qualifies as burdened, and HUD labels anything above 50% severely burdened. That threshold was built to flag households in housing distress for federal assistance programs, not to tell an individual renter what a comfortable budget looks like. Over the decades landlords, budgeting apps, and finance writers borrowed the number anyway. The original purpose, spotting severe cost burden for public assistance, got lost along the way. If you live in federally assisted housing, HUD's rules for verifying household members' eligible status change on December 14, 2026. Our guide to the HUD mixed-status housing rule explains who is affected. Why 30% Breaks Down in Expensive Cities The 30% rule stops working in any metro where the typical rent already costs more than 30% of the typical income. The U.S. Census Bureau tracks median gross rent as a share of household income every year. In cities like San Francisco, New York, Boston, and Miami, that ratio already runs well past 30% for a full-time worker earning the local median wage. The housing stock and the local wages simply do not line up. A renter in one of those cities faces a real choice. Spending above 30% is one option, and it does not mean the renter budgeted wrong. Taking on a roommate, moving farther out for a longer commute, or renting a smaller unit are the others, and each carries a real cost in money or time. Someone who insists on hitting 30% in a tight market pays for it another way. The same income buys a much smaller unit, or a much longer commute, than it would in a cheaper city. That is the actual tradeoff a tight rental market forces on every income level. It is not a sign the renter did the math wrong. Gross Income or Take-Home Pay Use your gross income, the amount before taxes, as the base for the 28% number, because that is what HUD's own standard and most lenders already use. Gross income also sits right on your pay stub, before your specific tax withholding and benefit deductions shrink it down. Using the same base as everyone else lets you compare your number to theirs. Gross income can flatter your situation, though, if you put a lot into a 401(k) or pay high health insurance premiums. Two people earning the same $70,000 salary can take home very different amounts once one maxes out retirement contributions. The safer move is a two-step check: run the 28/36 math on gross income first, then confirm the resulting rent still leaves room in your real take-home pay. If your paycheck already runs thin after taxes and deductions, treat take-home pay as the real ceiling. A rent can fit neatly under 28% of gross income and still be unsafe. If it eats half your real paycheck, the math on paper does not matter. Confirm the number against a full month of expenses with our budget calculators , not just the rent line by itself. How to Calculate Your Own Safe Rent Number Calculate your safe rent number with a 28/36 split on gross income: rent alone at or under 28%, and rent plus every other debt payment at or under 36%. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) calls this same math a debt-to-income ratio, the core test mortgage lenders use to size a home loan. The same math works just as well sized to a rent payment instead of a mortgage. Start with your gross monthly income before taxes, then multiply it by 0.28 to get your front-end limit, the most rent alone should ever take. Next, add up your other required monthly debt payments. That includes a car loan, student loans, credit cards, and anything else with a minimum due. Multiply your gross monthly income by 0.36, subtract those other debts from that number, and you have your back-end limit, the true ceiling once existing debt is counted. Your actual rent ceiling is whichever of the two numbers is lower, the flat 28% figure or the debt-adjusted back-end figure. Someone with no other debt can often afford close to 30% of gross income in rent and still stay under the back-end limit. Someone carrying a car payment and student loans needs a smaller rent number to keep total obligations under 36%, even on the exact same income. Worked Example at $50,000 and $90,000 A renter earning $50,000 a year has a gross monthly income of about $4,167. The 28% front-end limit puts rent at $1,167 a month. Add $350 a month in car and student loan payments, and the 36% back-end limit drops to $1,150, the lower number and the real ceiling. A renter earning $90,000 a year has a gross monthly income of $7,500. The 28% front-end limit puts rent at $2,100, and with no other debt the 36% back-end limit sits at $2,700, so $2,100 is the binding number. Add $600 a month in student loan and credit card payments and the back-end limit falls to exactly $2,100, matching the front-end figure for the first time. Add just $200 more in monthly debt beyond that $600, and the debt-adjusted ceiling drops to $1,900, below the plain 28% number. The pattern holds at both income levels. Debt does not just compete with rent for the same paycheck. It also lowers the safe rent number below what a flat percentage rule would suggest. Splitting Rent with Roommates or a Partner Split rent by income share, not straight down the middle, whenever two renters earn meaningfully different amounts. An even split can push the lower earner well past their own safe ceiling while the higher earner still has room to spare, even on identical rent. Add both incomes together, then give each person that same percentage of the rent. Two roommates earning $3,000 and $5,000 a month have a combined income of $8,000. The lower earner makes 37.5% of that total and pays 37.5% of the rent. The higher earner pays the remaining 62.5%. On a $2,000 rent, that puts $750 on the lower earner and $1,250 on the higher earner, instead of $1,000 apiece. Couples who merge finances often split everything down the middle out of habit. That habit can hurt when one partner earns far more. Run each partner's own 28/36 numbers before agreeing on a shared rent figure. Check the resulting share against a full budget with our 50/30/20 budget calculator . Once you have a rent number, take the rental checklist of what to check before you sign on tours, and use the first apartment checklist to total move-in costs. Who This Guidance Is Not For This math is not the right target for someone carrying a lot of high-interest debt, like several credit cards near their limit. That renter should aim well under 28% for rent, not the standard ceiling, and put the spare room toward the high-interest balance first. A rent that technically clears the 36% back-end limit still leaves too little breathing room when much of that 36% is a minimum payment that barely touches the principal. It also is not the right framework for irregular income. A commissioned salesperson or a freelancer with lumpy months needs a different approach. Averaging a strong year into one flat monthly figure hides the lean months. That average rent number can be more than a slow month can actually cover. That renter is better off sizing rent against a worst realistic month and keeping a larger cash cushion than this math assumes. What Would Change This Answer A rental market with almost no vacancy changes this math. The calculation assumes real options exist at more than one price point. When every unit in a safe price range draws a dozen applications, options narrow fast. The real choices become overpaying, adding a roommate, or waiting. In that market, treat the 28/36 numbers as a ceiling to negotiate toward, not a promise that something at that price is available. A near-term income change shifts the answer too. Someone starting a job with a signed raise has a case for stretching slightly above the ceiling. The same goes for someone expecting a second income within a few months. Take a short lease, then reassess the number at renewal. The reverse holds too. Anyone expecting a pay cut, a job change, or a return to school should budget toward the stricter end of the range, not the top of it. Run your own numbers again with our 50/30/20 budget calculator before you sign a lease near either edge of your range. Frequently asked questions What percentage of my income should go to rent? Rent should generally stay at or under 28% of your gross income, and less than that once other debt is factored in. This debt-adjusted version of the 30% rule catches a real problem the flat rule misses: two people with the same income but different debt loads need different rent ceilings. Run the 28/36 math on your own numbers before you commit to a lease. Where did the 30% rent rule come from? The 30% figure comes from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), which uses it as the threshold for what it calls cost-burdened housing in federal assistance programs. It was built to flag households in housing distress, not to set a personal budgeting target. That history is why the number does not always fit a renter's actual situation. Should I calculate rent based on gross income or take-home pay? Start with gross income, since that is the base HUD's standard and most lenders use for the 28/36 math. Then check the resulting rent against your real take-home pay, especially if you contribute heavily to a 401(k) or pay high health premiums. Whichever number leaves less room is the one to budget against. What should I do if rent in my city is more than 30% of my income? In a high-cost metro, treat 30% as a target to negotiate toward rather than a hard limit you can always hit. A roommate, a smaller unit, or a longer commute usually closes more of the gap than stretching your budget alone. Near-zero vacancy can make even those options scarce, so start the search early and set a backup price point. How should roommates split rent fairly? Split rent by income share rather than splitting it evenly, whenever incomes are meaningfully different. Add both incomes together, then give each roommate that same percentage of the total rent. This keeps the lower earner from carrying a share of rent that pushes past their own safe ceiling. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. But renting offers more flexibility and lower upfront costs, and it can be the better choice in high-price markets where monthly ownership costs far exceed rent for comparable properties. Renting vs Buying: Side-by-Side Renting Buying Upfront cost Low (first+last month, deposit ~$3–6k) High (3–20% down + 2–5% closing costs) Monthly cost Rent only (fixed term, may rise) Mortgage + taxes + insurance + maintenance Equity building None — money goes to landlord Yes — builds with each payment Flexibility to move High — relocate when lease ends Low — selling takes months + costs 6–10% Maintenance responsibility Landlord's (mostly) Owner's — budget 1% of home value/year Tax benefits None Mortgage interest + property tax deductions Break-even timeline N/A Depends on the mortgage rate and the price-to-rent ratio 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Rent when you plan to stay fewer than 5 years, value mobility, or live in a high-cost city where price-to-rent ratios are above 25x. Buy when you plan to stay 7+ years, have a stable income and emergency fund, and housing costs are reasonable relative to rent (price-to-rent ratio below 20x). The rent-vs-buy decision is more about your life stage than pure math. The true cost of buying a home Most people underestimate the true cost of homeownership. Beyond the mortgage payment, owners pay property taxes (typically 1–2% of home value per year), homeowner's insurance (~0.5–1%), HOA fees (if applicable), and maintenance — the standard rule is 1% of home value annually, but older homes can easily run 2–3%. On a $400,000 home with a 20% down payment, a 7% mortgage rate, 1.2% property tax, 0.8% insurance, and 1% maintenance, the true monthly cost is about $2,950 — before building any equity. After the equity portion, your actual 'rent equivalent' (the sunk cost) is closer to $2,200/month in the early years. The mortgage calculator and net worth calculator can help you model full ownership costs and how home equity builds your net worth over time. Why renting is not 'throwing money away' The most persistent myth in personal finance is that rent is wasted money. It's not — rent buys you housing, flexibility, freedom from maintenance, and the ability to deploy your down payment capital elsewhere. A $80,000 down payment invested in a diversified stock portfolio earning 8% annually grows to $860,000 over 30 years. That same $80,000 tied up as a down payment grows only as fast as home appreciation — historically 3–4% annually — reaching about $195,000 over 30 years. The gap closes when you factor in leverage (you control $400k of home with $80k), the forced savings effect of mortgage payments, and rent that would have otherwise exceeded mortgage costs. The math favors buying in low-to-moderate price markets and long holding periods. If you rent in federally assisted housing, HUD's eligibility-verification rules change on December 14, 2026. See how housing assistance rule changes affect renters. The price-to-rent ratio: your key metric The price-to-rent ratio is the clearest tool for the rent-vs-buy decision. Calculate it by dividing the home purchase price by the annual rent of a comparable property. A ratio below 15 favors buying when mortgage rates are low. A ratio of 15–20 is roughly neutral. Above 20, renting becomes increasingly competitive; above 25, renting usually wins financially. In 2024, San Francisco's price-to-rent ratio exceeds 40x — meaning a $1.5 million home rents for less than $40,000/year. Chicago and Cleveland run near 12–14x, clearly favoring buyers. Most U.S. metros fall between 15–25x. A practical non-obvious insight: the price-to-rent ratio also predicts your break-even point. A higher ratio pushes the break-even later, and a lower mortgage rate pulls it earlier. Rates move these numbers a lot: in our internal modeling, a $400,000 home renting for $2,200 (a ratio of 15.2) breaks even in year 5 at a 5% mortgage rate but in year 21 at 7.32%, which you can test in our rent vs buy calculator . When renting is the smarter financial move Renting is financially rational in several scenarios that many buyers overlook. When your job is unstable or you might relocate, selling a home within 2–3 years rarely recovers the 6–10% transaction costs (agent commissions, closing costs, repairs). You're often financially better renting and keeping capital flexible. Renting also makes sense during periods of elevated home prices and rates, when the monthly cost to own far exceeds rent. In many coastal markets in 2023–2024, buying required a 25–35% premium over renting comparable space — a drag that takes many years to overcome through appreciation. Renting in a high-rent area while house-hacking (buying a multi-unit property elsewhere and renting out units) is an increasingly popular strategy for building wealth without tying yourself to an expensive market. The rental property calculator can help evaluate investment property returns. If you rent, use the rental checklist of what to check before you sign and, for a first place, the first apartment checklist ; if you buy, start with the home buying checklist . Frequently asked questions Is renting or buying cheaper in 2024? In most U.S. markets in 2024, renting is cheaper on a monthly basis due to elevated home prices and 7%+ mortgage rates. However, buying builds equity while renting does not. The break-even point, when buying becomes the better financial deal, depends mainly on the mortgage rate and the price-to-rent ratio, and our rent vs buy calculator finds it for your numbers. How long should you own a home before selling? Financial planners generally recommend owning a home for at least 5–7 years before selling to recoup transaction costs (agent commissions, closing costs, repairs) through appreciation and equity buildup. Selling in fewer than 3 years often results in a net loss even in appreciating markets. What is the price-to-rent ratio? The price-to-rent ratio is the home purchase price divided by the annual rent of a comparable property. A ratio below 15 favors buying; above 20 favors renting. San Francisco exceeds 40x (strong rent signal); Cleveland runs near 12x (strong buy signal). Does renting build wealth? Renting itself doesn't build wealth — but investing the down payment and payment difference in the stock market can. In high price-to-rent ratio markets, renting and investing the capital often outperforms buying, especially over short-to-medium time horizons.
